verses.text: Adam, Seth, Enosh,
Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared,
Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech,
Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
The sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras.
The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Diphath, and Togarmah.
The sons of Javan: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Rodanim.
The sons of Ham: Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan.
The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabta, Raama, Sabteca. The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan.
Cush became the father of Nimrod. He began to be a mighty one in the earth.
Mizraim became the father of Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim,
Pathrusim, Casluhim (where the Philistines came from), and Caphtorim.
Canaan became the father of Sidon his firstborn, Heth,
the Jebusite, and the Amorite, the Girgashite,
the Hivite, the Arkite, the Sinite,
the Arvadite, the Zemarite, and the Hamathite.
The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, Aram, Uz, Hul, Gether, and Meshech.
Arpachshad became the father of Shelah, and Shelah became the father of Eber.
To Eber were born two sons: the name of the one was Peleg, for in his days the earth was divided; and his brother’s name was Joktan.
Joktan became the father of Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah,
Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah,
Ebal, Abimael, Sheba,
Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. All these were the sons of Joktan.
Shem, Arpachshad, Shelah,
Eber, Peleg, Reu,
Serug, Nahor, Terah,
Abram (also called Abraham).
The sons of Abraham: Isaac and Ishmael.
These are their generations: the firstborn of Ishmael, Nebaioth; then Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam,
Mishma, Dumah, Massa, Hadad, Tema,
Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah. These are the sons of Ishmael.
The sons of Keturah, Abraham’s concubine: she bore Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. The sons of Jokshan: Sheba and Dedan.
The sons of Midian: Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the sons of Keturah.
Abraham became the father of Isaac. The sons of Isaac: Esau and Israel.
The sons of Esau: Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jalam, and Korah.
The sons of Eliphaz: Teman, Omar, Zephi, Gatam, Kenaz, Timna, and Amalek.
The sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah.
The sons of Seir: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan.
The sons of Lotan: Hori and Homam; and Timna was Lotan’s sister.
The sons of Shobal: Alian, Manahath, Ebal, Shephi, and Onam. The sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah.
The son of Anah: Dishon. The sons of Dishon: Hamran, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran.
The sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Jaakan. The sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran.
Now these are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the children of Israel: Bela the son of Beor; and the name of his city was Dinhabah.
Bela died, and Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his place.
Jobab died, and Husham of the land of the Temanites reigned in his place.
Husham died, and Hadad the son of Bedad, who struck Midian in the field of Moab, reigned in his place; and the name of his city was Avith.
Hadad died, and Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his place.
Samlah died, and Shaul of Rehoboth by the River reigned in his place.
Shaul died, and Baal Hanan the son of Achbor reigned in his place.
Baal Hanan died, and Hadad reigned in his place; and the name of his city was Pai: and his wife’s name was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred, the daughter of Mezahab.
Then Hadad died. The chiefs of Edom were: chief Timna, chief Aliah, chief Jetheth,
chief Oholibamah, chief Elah, chief Pinon,
chief Kenaz, chief Teman, chief Mibzar,
chief Magdiel, and chief Iram. These are the chiefs of Edom.

footnotes.content: Adam named first—not as a hero, but as the one through whom sin entered the world. Yet in Jesus, a second Adam came to undo what the first broke. That's how God reads the family tree.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seth, chosen in Adam's place. The genealogies skip over Cain's line—God sees the faithful ones, not the proud. These names trace a thread of faith reaching toward the promise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Enoch walked with God and was taken. Methuselah's long life spanned the faith of Noah's grandfather. Even when the world grew wicked, God kept a line of witnesses.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Noah saved through the flood, his three sons become the seed of all nations. God didn't destroy His people—He preserved them. From one faithful man, the whole earth was repeopled.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Japheth's sons settled in the northward lands—the Gentile nations. The family tree spreads outward; God's plan has always been wider than Israel alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gomer and Togarmah—names that trace into the distant peoples. God sees them all by name, even before nations form and borders shift.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Javan, Tarshish, Kittim—names of seafaring peoples and trade routes. The chronicle shows how God's family scatters across the whole earth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ham's sons include Egypt, Ethiopia, and Canaan—nations vital to Israel's story. Some will be enemies, others neighbors; all are in God's sight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sheba and Dedan—the trader-names of Arabia. The genealogy isn't just names; it's the memory of peoples and their lands, all woven into one family story.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nimrod 'began to be mighty'—first hunter, first to build the tower of Babel. When pride grows, God scatters. His power alone is lasting.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mizraim fathered Egypt—land of plagues and slavery where Israel's story will be tested and refined. Every name holds a chapter of God's unfolding purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Philistines came from Casluhim—those who will harass Israel for generations. Yet even enemies are part of the record, part of how God shapes His people through struggle.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sidon—Canaan's firstborn, an ancient city. Its people will trade, build, and later meet the prophets. Every name carries the weight of generations to come.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Amorite, the Jebusite—peoples Israel will face as enemies in Canaan. They too came from Noah's line; they too could have chosen the Lord's way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Hivite, the Arkite—tribal names that will mark battles and boundaries. God knows each one; they matter to His story even when their names fade from memory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Arvadite, Zemarite, Hamathite—coastal and inland peoples, merchants and warriors. The genealogy frames the map of all Israel will inherit.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shem's sons lean eastward—Asshur, Aram, the heartland of the Middle East. From Shem comes Abraham's line; the elect run through this branch.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Arpachshad → Shelah → Eber. These links reach forward: Eber is father of Peleg, who will see the earth divided at Babel. Long chains of purpose, held fast by God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peleg—'the earth was divided' in his days. Babel's confusion, yet God chose one man's line through which the promise would flow unbroken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joktan and his sons spread toward Arabia. Even those who diverge from the main line of promise are held in God's memory, seen by His eye.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: More names of Arabia's peoples, merchants and desert dwellers. The genealogy spans the known world—God's purposes embrace all nations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ophir's name will later echo as a land of gold and treasure. Names carry their meanings through time; God weaves all stories into one tapestry.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'All these were the sons of Joktan'—a summary pause. Even lines that don't lead to Israel are honored in the record. God misses no one.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now the thread narrows—Shem's descendants in their order. The chronicle begins to follow the line of the covenant more closely, step by step toward Abraham.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eber, Peleg, Reu—names of patience and duration. Each lived and waited; each passed the promise to the next. Faith waits; it does not rush.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Serug, Nahor, Terah—the line tightens. Terah will carry his son Abram from Ur; the promise moves nearer with each generation named.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abram—also called Abraham. The name change marks a threshold: he is renamed in covenant, called to be father of nations. From here, the genealogy becomes the covenant family.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac and Ishmael—both sons of Abraham, yet Isaac carries the promise forward. Both matter; not all children of the flesh are children of the covenant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ishmael's firstborn, Nebaioth—his line receives honor in the record, even though the covenant flows through Isaac. God blesses both, though the promise goes one way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Kedar—later a name for Arabian peoples. Even those outside the covenant line are numbered and remembered; God sees and honors all His creatures.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'These are the sons of Ishmael'—a summary. The blessing spreads wide; the covenant thread stays narrow and sure, bound for Israel.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Keturah's sons—Abraham, though old, still fathers more. His fruitfulness echoes the promise; offspring like stars, though the covenant line is singular.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Midian—later a nation Israel will meet in the wilderness and at Judges' courts. Abraham's grandchildren spread across the lands where God will later work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abraham → Isaac; Isaac → Esau and Jacob (Israel). The narrowing continues. Jacob is renamed 'Israel'; from him the twelve tribes and the covenant people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esau's sons—he chose the earthly promise over the spiritual. His line becomes Edom, rival and neighbor to Israel; both brothers' descendants will fill the earth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eliphaz's children include Amalek—later Israel's archetypal enemy. From Esau's line comes one who will test Israel's faith and courage for generations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Reuel's sons continue Esau's line. All named, all real; the genealogy honors Edom even as it traces the covenant through Jacob.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seir the Horite—the peoples of the hill country before Israel enters. Geography and genealogy twine together; the land itself was inhabited.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Timna was Lotan's sister—the chronicle names both men and women, honoring how relationships bind families. Every person has a place in God's story.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shobal and Zibeon's descendants fill the early Edomite lands. These names anchor a region where Esau's children made their home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Anah fathered Dishon—genealogies are chains, each link in place. The specificity honors the reality that God works through real, named, interconnected people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ezer and Dishan's sons—more names of Edom's clans. Every valley and tribe in that land had fathers and families; all are written down before God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Kings reigned in Edom 'before any king reigned over the children of Israel.' Edom organized under monarchy first; Israel would follow later, shaped by its own covenant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Kings rise and fall in Edom, each remembered in turn. Human kingship is brief; the kingdom of God endures forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Husham of the Temanites—the cycle continues. One king dies, another takes the throne. Yet through it all, Israel's God is building toward His purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hadad struck Midian in Moab's field. Edom's kings wage wars; the land is contested. God's people will later know this same struggle.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Samlah of Masrekah—each name a dynasty, each king a chapter in Edom's story. None of their great deeds saves them from the grave.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shaul of Rehoboth—a kingdom by the river, a city named. Power and possession pass like morning mist.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Baal Hanan—the name carries hints of false gods; still, even kings who chase idols are numbered in the record. God's patience is longer than any reign.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hadad reigned again; his wife named Mehetabel. Even marriages and dynasties are briefly sketched. Life unfolds in names; eternity belongs to God alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Then Hadad died.' The turning point: kings end, and chieftains rise. Edom's glory shifts from centralized rule to tribal leaders.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon—Edom's chiefs, each commanding a region. Power disperses; authority scatters among the clans.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar—more chiefs, more territories. Each name holds land and people; each is a thread in the tapestry Edom weaves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Magdiel, Iram—the final chiefs of Edom. Readers today hear an echo in these names: all kingdoms rise and pass away, save One. Every genealogy points toward the King who never dies.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
